blocks.text: The theory of relativity deals with how observers in different states of relative motion describe physical phenomena. The special theory of relativity addresses problems involving inertial (non-accelerating) frames of reference. Another theory, the general theory of relativity, deals with problems involving frames of reference that are accelerating relative to one another. The special theory is based on two postulates:

items: The laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames (principle of relativity).
The speed of light in free space has the same value for all observers, regardless of the state of motion of the source or the observer (principle of constancy of light).

blocks.text: The first postulate generalizes the fact that all physical laws are the same in frames of reference moving with uniform velocity relative to one another. If the laws of physics differed for observers in relative motion, those observers could determine which was stationary and which was moving; no such distinction exists, so there is no way to detect absolute uniform motion. The second postulate states the experimental fact that the speed of light in free space is a universal constant, c = 3 x 10^8 m s^-1; the speed of light from a torch is measured the same by an observer in a car moving with speed v and by one standing on the road (Do You Know).

Since c is constant, space and time become relative. For example, if you sat in a train moving close to the speed of light and held up a mirror at arm's length, you would still see your reflection, because by the principle of relativity no experiment can detect the constant motion of the train relative to the person inside it. These simple postulates have far-reaching consequences, such as the slowing down of clocks and the contraction of lengths in moving frames as observed by a stationary observer.

If two events in different locations are observed by one observer to be simultaneous, they will generally not be simultaneous for another observer in a frame moving relative to the first. Consider a train with light-operated doors and a light switch in the centre of the roof, operated by a traveller standing in the middle of the compartment. When the train travels at half the speed of light, the traveller turns on the light. The light travels forward and backward at equal speed and reaches both doors at the same time, so the traveller sees both doors open simultaneously. An observer outside the train, however, sees the back door open before the front door, because the back door is moving towards the light waves while the front door is moving away from them. If you are in a frame moving at constant velocity from which you cannot see any other frame, there is no way to know whether you are moving or at rest (Interesting Information).

According to the special theory of relativity, time is not an absolute quantity; it depends on the motion of the frame of reference. Suppose an observer at rest in an inertial frame measures the time interval t0 between two events in that frame; this is the proper time. If the observer moves relative to the frame of the events with relativistic velocity v, or the frame of the events moves relative to the observer, the time measured is not t0 but t = t0/sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) ... (11.1). As sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) is always less than one, t is greater than t0: time is dilated, or stretched, by the relative motion. This applies to all timing processes, physical, chemical and biological; even the ageing of the human body is slowed at relativistic speeds. For example, if a traveller on a plane moving at 0.8c opens a book in one second as measured by the traveller, the same event takes 1.7 s for a person standing outside the plane.

The distance from the Earth to a star measured by an observer in a moving spaceship appears smaller than the distance measured by an observer on the Earth. If you move relative to two points a fixed distance apart, the distance between them appears shorter than if you were at rest relative to them; this is length contraction. It occurs only along the direction of motion; no contraction is observed perpendicular to it. The length measured by an observer at rest relative to the object is the proper length l0. If the object and the observer are in relative motion with speed v, the contracted length is l = l0 sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) ... (11.2). A train 100 m long at rest, travelling at 0.8c, is still 100 m to a person inside, but a person beside the track measures only 60 m.

According to the special theory of relativity, the mass of an object depends on its speed. An object whose mass measured at rest is m0 (its rest mass) has an increased mass m when observed moving at speed v: m = m0/sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) ... (11.3). The increase in mass means an increase in inertia at high speeds: as v approaches c, a greater force is needed to change the speed. As v tends to c, v/c tends to 1 and sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) tends to 0, so m tends to infinity. An infinite mass would need an infinite force to accelerate it; since infinite forces are not available, a material object cannot be accelerated to the speed of light in free space.

In everyday life we deal with speeds that are extremely small compared with the speed of light; even the Earth's orbital speed is only 30 km s^-1, while light travels at 300 000 km s^-1. That is why Newton's laws are valid in everyday situations. For subatomic particles moving at speeds approaching that of light, relativistic effects become very prominent, and experimental results cannot be explained without Einstein's equations.

blocks.caption: Consequences of special relativity, mass-energy and curved space-time (original diagram after Figure 11.2 and topics 11.3 to 11.5).
blocks.long_description: At everyday speeds the relativistic factors are almost exactly one, but as the speed approaches that of light the factor one over the square root of one minus v squared over c squared grows without limit: a moving clock is seen to run slow by this factor, a moving mass to grow by it, and a moving length to shrink by its inverse; at 0.8c the factors are 1.67 and 0.6. Energy and mass are linked by E equals m c squared. In Einstein's picture a massive body curves space-time like a heavy ball on a stretched sheet, and bodies and light follow the curves; starlight passing the Sun is bent, so the star appears slightly shifted, as measured in the 1919 eclipse.

blocks.title: Example 11.1
blocks.text: The period of a pendulum is measured to be 3.0 s in the inertial frame of the pendulum. What is its period measured by an observer moving at 0.95c with respect to the pendulum? Solution: t0 = 3.0 s, v = 0.95c. t = t0/sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) = 3.0 s/sqrt(1 - (0.95)^2) = 9.6 s.

blocks.title: Example 11.2
blocks.text: A bar 1.0 m long, lying along the x-axis, moves with a speed of 0.75c with respect to a stationary observer. What is its length as measured by the stationary observer? Solution: l0 = 1.0 m, v = 0.75c. l = l0 sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) = 1.0 m x sqrt(1 - (0.75)^2) = 0.66 m.

blocks.title: Example 11.3
blocks.text: Find the mass m of an object moving with speed 0.8c. Solution: m = m0/sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) = m0/sqrt(1 - (0.8)^2) = 1.67 m0.
